The {#}s
The post-war boom ended. Prices rose sharply and the pound was unstable, causing balance of payments problems (imports worth more than exports).
Many strikes; people argued the trade unions were too powerful.
Serious unrest in Northern Ireland: in 1972 its Parliament was suspended and it was ruled directly from London. Some 3,000 people died in the violence in the decades after 1969.
Europe: West Germany, France, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands formed the EEC in 1957. The UK joined in 1973. It never used the Euro, and left the EU in 2020.
Conservative government {#}–{#}
Margaret Thatcher, the first woman PM, led from 1979 to 1990.
Privatisation of nationalised industries and legal controls on trade union powers.
Deregulation grew the City of London as a centre for investment, insurance and finance. Traditional industries such as shipbuilding and coal mining declined.
In 1982 Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands; a naval taskforce recovered them.
John Major followed Thatcher and helped establish the Northern Ireland peace process.
Labour government {#}–{#}
Tony Blair’s government introduced a Scottish Parliament (substantial law-making powers) and a Welsh Assembly (fewer legislative powers but considerable control over public services).
The Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998. The Northern Ireland Assembly was elected in 1999, suspended in 2002 and reinstated in 2007. Most paramilitary groups have decommissioned their arms.
Gordon Brown became PM in {#}.
Conflicts abroad
In the 1990s Britain helped liberate Kuwait after Iraq invaded in 1990, and took part in the conflict in the former Republic of Yugoslavia.
Since 2000, British forces have fought international terrorism and the spread of weapons of mass destruction, in Afghanistan and Iraq. Combat troops left Iraq in 2009.
In Afghanistan the UK served in the UN-mandated, 50-nation ISAF coalition, building up Afghan security forces, with full Afghan responsibility by the end of 2014.
Recent governments
In May 2010 no party won an overall majority, for the first time since February 1974. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed a coalition under David Cameron.

Conservative governments 2015–2024 had five PMs: David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak. Events included the 2016 EU referendum (Brexit) and the COVID-19 pandemic. Sunak called an election for 4 July 2024.
Labour, led by Keir Starmer, won a majority in the 2024 general election.

An imaginary machine reads a long tape divided into squares.
Each square holds a symbol, such as {#} or {#}.
Following a short list of rules, the head reads a symbol, writes a new one and moves left or right.
Turing showed that a machine like this can carry out any calculation: the idea behind every modern computer.
Suck: a fan at the front draws air in.
Squeeze: the compressor squeezes the air tightly.
Bang: fuel is sprayed in and burnt, so the hot gas expands with great force.
Blow: the gas rushes out of the back, spinning a turbine on its way and pushing the aircraft forwards.
A transmitter sends out short pulses of radio waves.
The waves bounce off an aircraft and an echo comes back.
The time the echo takes shows how far away the aircraft is; the direction of the aerial shows where it is.
The aircraft appears as a “blip” on a screen, even at night or in cloud.
Stars, galaxies and other objects in space give off faint radio waves.
The huge bowl-shaped dish collects the waves over a wide area.
The dish reflects them to a receiver held at its focus.
Computers turn the signals into maps of the sky. Lovell’s telescope at Jodrell Bank, Cheshire, was for many years the biggest in the world.
Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas.
It works like a key, letting the body’s cells take in sugar from the blood for energy.
In diabetes the body does not make or use enough insulin, so sugar builds up in the blood.
Injections of insulin keep blood sugar under control.
DNA is the molecule that carries the instructions for every living thing.
Its shape is a “double helix”: two strands twisted like a spiral staircase.
The “steps” are pairs of chemical bases that spell out the genetic code.
Knowing the structure led to many advances, especially in medicine and in fighting crime.
A powerful fan blows air down underneath the craft.
A flexible rubber “skirt” around the edge traps the air, making a cushion.
The craft floats on this cushion just above land or water, so there is very little friction.
Propellers push it forwards.
A supersonic airliner: it flew faster than the speed of sound.
Its slim triangular “delta” wings suited very high speeds.
The long nose drooped down for take-off and landing so the pilots could see the runway.
It carried passengers from 1976 until it was retired in 2003.
Take off
Fly forwards
The engine’s thrust comes out of four nozzles that can swivel.
Pointing the nozzles down lifts the aircraft straight up: vertical take-off.
Swivelling them backwards pushes it forwards like a normal jet.
It can take off from small clearings or ships instead of long runways.
You put in a bank card that identifies your account.
You type a secret PIN (personal identification number) to prove it is you.
The machine checks with the bank’s computer that there is enough money.
It counts out the cash. The first was used by Barclays in Enfield, north London, in 1967.
IVF means in-vitro fertilisation: fertilisation “in glass”, outside the body.
An egg and sperm are brought together in a laboratory dish.
The fertilised egg divides into two cells, then four, then more: an early embryo.
The embryo is placed in the mother’s womb to grow. The first “test-tube baby” was born in Oldham in 1978.
The patient lies inside a large, very strong magnet.
The magnet lines up tiny particles in the water in the body.
Radio pulses knock them out of line; as they settle back they give off signals.
A computer turns the signals into detailed pictures of the organs inside, without surgery.
Web pages are stored on computers called servers, connected through the internet.
Every page has an address and can link to any other page.
Clicking a link asks the server for that page, and your browser shows it.
Information was first transferred via the web on 25 December 1990.
A cell was taken from sheep A.
An egg was taken from sheep B and its nucleus (its DNA) removed.
The two were joined using a tiny electric pulse and grew into an embryo.
Sheep C gave birth to Dolly, a genetic copy of sheep A: the first cloned mammal.
